paras: The threatened lynching of Jim Montgomery occurred at Lowrysville (also spelled Lowryville), Chester County, South Carolina, on the night of May 4, 1903, when a crowd was reported gathering to lynch Montgomery, a Black man arrested on the accusation of threatening an aged widow with a pistol. Governor Heyward sent the Lee Light Infantry by special train, and the sheriff took the prisoner to the Chester jail without resistance. A Columbia dispatch credited the militia with probably preventing a lynching, while a Chester correspondent called the report "greatly exaggerated"; later reports named the man Jim Gilmore.

According to the Chester Lantern, at about 1 a.m. on May 4 someone raised a window at the house of Mrs. Neely Smith, presented a pistol and declared he would shoot if anyone raised an alarm. Her granddaughter, Mamie Hardin, ran to call neighbors, and the intruder fled.

After daylight a track was followed to Will Simpson's place, where Montgomery was arrested because his shoes were believed to match it; the Columbia State's correspondent instead said he was "tracked and caught about dark." He was "locked up in a store and surrounded by armed men" and held until night, when a lynching was feared.

At the request of Solicitor Henry, the governor placed the Lee Light Infantry, 42 strong, under Sheriff Cornwell, and the company went to Lowrysville by special train. The troops did not find a large crowd, and "no demonstration whatever was made"; the sheriff claimed his prisoner and jailed him for trial at the next term of court. The Lantern said he was reported to have confessed "at the point of a pistol" but "persistently denied that he knew anything about the deed."

In June 1903 the Columbia Record reported that Jim Gilmore, the man the militia had protected at Lowryville, had broken out of the Chester jail with Will Talbert and robbed the Lowryville post office. A Lowryville letter said the pair broke into R. T. Sandifer's store, and Sheriff Cornwell offered a $10 reward for each. The Record put the state's cost for two days of military service and the special train at about $175.
In May 1904 Sheriff Logan captured Gilmore at a saw mill near King's Mountain and returned him to Chester; no report of a trial was found.

The version that traveled furthest was the Columbia dispatch of May 5, printed in the Savannah Morning News as "LYNCHING THREATENED" and in the Atlanta Constitution and Keowee Courier as "Troops Are Guarding Negro." It stated the accusation as fact and credited the militia's "prompt arrival" with probably preventing the lynching. Closer to the scene, the Columbia State's correspondent ran "LYNCHING DID NOT OCCUR," said troops were sought "to preserve Chester's reputation against all kinds of lawlessness," and called Montgomery "a burly young negro."

The Anderson Mail, reprinted in the Keowee Courier and Lexington Dispatch, could not feel "a great deal of pleasure" at troops called out "to protect a negro who attempts an assault upon a white woman." After the jail break the Lancaster Enterprise's Lowryville correspondent called Gilmore "desperate" and wrote that such escapes "make men slow to commit such characters to the jail." All coverage found came from white Southern papers; none was found in the Black press.

The May reports name the man Jim Montgomery, while those of June 1903 and May 1904 name him Jim Gilmore; no article reconciles the names. The accusation shifted from a pistol at a window in the Lantern to an attempted assault on a white woman in the Anderson Mail and a break-in at a house of "unprotected ladies" in 1904. The danger also varies: a mob in the dispatch, a small crowd with few "violently disposed" in the local reports, and troops needed at the Chester jail in the 1904 account.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Jim Montgomery
bases: A crowd was reported gathering to lynch an arrested Black man and troops were sent to prevent it (A1, A2, A3); no one was killed, so this is a threatened lynching.

No one was killed: the sheriff took the prisoner to jail without resistance (A3, A2), so the episode is at most a threatened lynching whose crowd the local reports called small (A2, A3); the pretext was a crime accusation (A1, A2).

The Columbia wire (A1) and two separate local accounts (A2 Chester Lantern, A3 Columbia State correspondent) agree on the arrest, the feared lynching and the militia call, though A3 calls the mob report 'greatly exaggerated' and A2 found few 'violently disposed'.

accounts.label: Columbia wire
accounts.gist: A mob gathered at Lowrysville to lynch Jim Montgomery, who had entered an aged widow's home and threatened to kill her; the prompt arrival of 42 militiamen probably prevented the lynching.

accounts.label: Chester Lantern
accounts.gist: An intruder threatened with a pistol at a window and fled; Montgomery was arrested on a track, held until night when lynching was feared, and taken to jail by troops who found no large crowd; he denied the deed.

accounts.label: Columbia State correspondent at Chester
accounts.gist: The lynching report was greatly exaggerated; the prisoner was held in a store by armed men, no demonstration was made and the sheriff took him without resistance.

accounts.label: Later reports on Jim Gilmore
accounts.gist: The man protected by the militia at Lowryville was Jim Gilmore, who 'barely escaped being lynched', broke jail in June 1903 and was recaptured in 1904.

framing.detail: Headlines 'LYNCHING THREATENED' and 'Troops Are Guarding Negro'; states the accusation as fact and credits the militia with preventing a lynching.
Columbia State correspondent: 'LYNCHING DID NOT OCCUR'; troops sought 'to preserve Chester's reputation against all kinds of lawlessness'; calls Montgomery 'a burly young negro'.
Anderson Mail editorial cannot feel 'a great deal of pleasure' that the lynching was prevented, given troops protecting 'a negro who attempts an assault upon a white woman'.
June reports call Gilmore 'costly' and 'desperate'; the Lowryville correspondent says escapes make men 'slow to commit such characters to the jail'.

conflicts.note: May 1903 reports say Montgomery; June 1903 and May 1904 reports say the man protected at Lowryville was Gilmore. No article reconciles the names.
